By two o’clock the streets around the palace were thick with soldiers, and the crowd that had gathered since morning had grown quiet in the way of a crowd that is waiting for something to break. Delegates hurried through the corridors carrying papers; messengers ran in with news that the telegraph office had changed hands, that the bridges were held, that the ministers had been arrested. In the great hall a speaker rose and read the decree on land, and the room, which a moment before had been full of argument, fell completely silent. When the vote was called, there was one voice against. Then the cheering began — a long rolling noise that seemed to fill the whole building — and men who had not slept for three days embraced one another like brothers.
